posts.style: Design & Aspiration · The Putting Green You Walk Down To
posts.alt: A Fairbanks Ranch Spanish Colonial estate backyard at golden hour: sand stucco and a clay barrel-tile roof over an arched loggia with a stacked-stone fireplace, linen lounge seating and a stainless outdoor kitchen island, a silver travertine terrace stepping down to a contoured putting green with two flags, olive trees, agave and low path lights; neighboring tile-roof estate homes sit close by on both sides and beyond the wall
posts.hook: The best view in a big backyard is usually the one you walk toward, not the one you sit and look at.
posts.caption:
Most putting greens get dropped into the corner of a yard like an afterthought. This one is the destination.

Stand in the loggia by the fire and the whole property reads in order: the stone hearth behind you, a travertine terrace in front, three wide steps down, and a contoured green with a soft fringe that pulls you out onto the grass. Olive trees hold the edges. Agave and rosemary keep the planting quiet so the green stays the focus.

The kitchen sits under the roofline, so whoever is cooking is a few steps from the game and the fire. Everything is within reach, nothing is crowded.

The selections:
• SYNLawn Golf putting green with contoured fringe
• Bedrosians silver travertine terrace & steps
• Eldorado Stone stacked-stone fireplace
• Lynx built-in grill in a stucco kitchen island
• olive, agave & rosemary · FX Luminaire path lighting

posts.style: Seasonal · First of December · Driveway & Curb Appeal · The Motor Court
posts.alt: The front of a single-story Mediterranean ranch home in Bonita at dusk in early December: sand stucco and terracotta tile roof, warm light in the windows, a natural evergreen and olive-branch wreath on the wood front door, a circular motor court of tumbled grey pavers around a planted island with a mature olive tree wrapped in soft white lights, a curved paver walk, boxwood, rosemary and lavender with low path lights; neighboring homes sit close by on both sides
posts.hook: December in San Diego doesn't need much. A good light, an old olive tree and a front door worth walking to.
posts.caption:
The holidays arrive at the front of the house first. Before anyone sees the table or the tree, they see the drive, the walk and the door.

This front yard is built to look good in December without trying hard. A circular motor court of tumbled pavers gives the drive a graceful turn instead of a flat slab, and a mature olive in the center island does the work of a hundred decorations. A few warm lights wrapped on the trunk, uplights on the tree and the stucco, low lights along the curved walk, one simple wreath on the door. Then the planting, clipped boxwood, rosemary and lavender, is still green and fragrant whatever the month.

Restraint is what makes it feel like a home and not a display.

The selections:
• Techo-Bloc Aberdeen tumbled pavers · motor court & curved walk
• mature olive tree in a planted island
• boxwood, rosemary & lavender
• FX Luminaire uplighting & path lights

posts.style: Process Carousel · Property Walk to Built
posts.alt: Four-slide SDLR process carousel of one Tierrasanta tract-home backyard between neighboring houses: the existing yard at the property walk with a cracked slab, an old rusted patio cover and dry lawn, the full 3D design render with louvered pergola, outdoor kitchen, fire pit and curving turf, a hand-rendered overhead design drawing of the same layout, and the finished build photographed at golden hour
posts.hook: Here's how a backyard goes from “it's fine, I guess” to built, without a single guess along the way.
posts.caption:
Most yards don't need more ideas. They need an order of operations, especially on a normal lot with neighbors a fence-width away.

Swipe through how our design process works, start to finish:

1. The property walk: we start with what's really there. The cracked slab, the grade, the sun, the view you want to keep and the one you don't.
2. The 3D design: the whole space modeled so you can see the pergola, the kitchen, the fire and the lawn in place, and change anything before it's real.
3. The drawing: every edge, level and planting resolved on paper, so the crew builds exactly what you approved. Client details stay private.
4. The build: and it matches, because nothing was left to be figured out in the field.

The render is the design. The last slide is the build. The point is that they look the same.

The selections:
• Belgard Urbana paver patio
• StruXure louvered pergola
• Eldorado Stone outdoor kitchen with Lynx built-in grill & bar
• Warming Trends fire pit with curved seat wall
• SYNLawn turf · olive, agave & lavender in raised planters

posts.alt: An Otay Ranch desert-modern backyard at dusk behind a contemporary two-story home with glowing glass doors: a warm grey porcelain patio, a long linear gas fire table lit at the center of a teak and cream lounge group, Corten steel planters with agave, golden barrel cactus and red yucca, a board-formed concrete seat wall and gravel; neighboring two-story homes sit close by beyond the block wall
posts.hook: The first cool evening of the year is when a backyard proves whether it was built to be used.
posts.caption:
By December the sun is down before dinner and the air has an edge. Plenty of yards go quiet right about now. This one gets going.

A long fire table does the work a campfire used to, with a seating group wrapped around it close enough to share the warmth. Behind it, the glass doors glow into the yard so the house and the patio feel like one room. Corten planters of agave, golden barrel and red yucca hold their shape in every season, and the board-formed seat wall gives a late guest somewhere to land.

Nothing here depends on summer. That's the idea: a yard you use in all twelve months.

The selections:
• Warming Trends linear gas fire table
• Belgard Porcelain patio in warm grey
• board-formed concrete seat wall
• Corten steel planters · agave, golden barrel & red yucca
• FX Luminaire accent lighting

posts.style: Trust & Difference · Coastal Pool · One Contract, One Firm
posts.alt: A Coronado backyard at golden hour behind a coastal contemporary white shingle home with a standing-seam metal roof: a rectangular pool with a raised spa and sheer water spill, a pale porcelain deck, a pergola-covered lounge, clipped hedges, queen palms, olive and grasses with a low stone wall; neighboring coastal homes sit close by on both sides with bay light in the sky
posts.hook: A pool is never one project. It's six trades that all have to agree on the same inch.
posts.caption:
Behind every pool that looks effortless is a schedule where the excavator, the shell, the plumber, the electrician, the stone setter and the planter all had to arrive in the right order and agree on the same finished height.

We build pools, and we run all of it under one contract. The pool shell is carried by a licensed specialty subcontractor, the same way every other trade on the job is, and we're the firm accountable for the whole result. You aren't refereeing a pool company against a hardscape company over coping height or deck level. You talk to Gio and Mike, and the plan stays one plan.

That's why the deck meets the coping cleanly, the spa spills where it should, and the planting lands where the pool left room for it.

The selections:
• Belgard Porcelain pool deck
• raised spa with sheer-descent spill
• Trex Pergola over the lounge
• queen palms, olive & ornamental grasses
• Kichler bronze path lighting

Thinking about a pool and everything around it? DM “DESIGN”.
